title: Thyroid storm
subject: endocrinology
summary: Clinical diagnosis aided by the Burch-Wartofsky score (45 or more) or JTA/JES criteria; treat in HDU or ICU with beta-blockade, high-dose thionamide, iodine at least 1 hour after the thionamide, hydrocortisone, cooling and treatment of the precipitant.

sections.title: Recognise and score
items: Severe thyrotoxicosis with decompensation: fever (often above 38.5 C), tachycardia out of proportion to fever, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, agitation, delirium, seizure or coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice. Older patients may present apathetic with few adrenergic signs.

Burch-Wartofsky score (temperature, CNS, GI-hepatic, heart rate, heart failure, AF, precipitant): 45 or more highly suggestive; 25 to 44 impending storm (decide on aggressive treatment with a senior clinician and endocrinologist); below 25 unlikely.

JTA/JES criteria need raised FT3 or FT4. Definite (TS1): a CNS feature plus one of fever 38 C or more, heart rate 130 or more, heart failure or GI/hepatic features (bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL or more), OR three non-CNS features. Suspected (TS2): two non-CNS features.

Precipitants: stopping antithyroid drugs, infection, surgery, trauma, childbirth, DKA, MI, stroke, iodinated contrast, radioiodine. Usual cause is Graves disease; also toxic nodular goitre and thyroiditis.
Differentials: sepsis, heat stroke, sympathomimetic toxicity (cocaine, amphetamines), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, encephalitis. Scores overlap with sepsis in ICU; use clinical judgement.

sections.title: Investigations (do not delay treatment)
items: FT4, FT3, TSH; CBC, liver function (bilirubin and transaminases guide PTU versus methimazole), electrolytes, glucose, calcium, CK, lactate, blood and urine cultures.
ECG and continuous monitoring, chest X-ray, early echocardiography (thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy, output state); pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.
Later for cause: TSH receptor antibodies, thyroid ultrasound. There is no hormone level that separates storm from uncomplicated severe thyrotoxicosis.

sections.title: Immediate treatment
items: Manage in HDU or ICU. ICU for vasopressor need, reduced consciousness, respiratory support, heart failure or shock, arrhythmia or multi-organ dysfunction. Alert surgeons early in case thyroidectomy is needed.

Beta-blockade: propranolol 60 to 80 mg orally every 4 hours (ATA and ETA) in stable patients without LV dysfunction. With heart failure, hypotension or suspected cardiomyopathy use short-acting IV esmolol (JTA/JES prefer beta1-selective agents: esmolol, landiolol, bisoprolol 2.5 to 5 mg/day).

Thionamide as soon as possible: methimazole 60 to 80 mg/day or carbimazole 80 to 100 mg/day in divided doses, OR propylthiouracil 500 to 1000 mg loading dose then 250 mg every 4 hours (oral, NG or rectal). Prefer methimazole or carbimazole if bilirubin or transaminases exceed 3 times normal.

Iodine at least 1 hour AFTER the thionamide: Lugol's iodine 8 drops four times daily or SSKI 5 drops four times daily, diluted in milk or juice. Omit in thyroiditis, amiodarone type 2 thyrotoxicosis and iodine allergy.
Glucocorticoid: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours (300 mg/day; JTA/JES) or dexamethasone 8 mg/day. The 2026 ETA/BTA consensus uses hydrocortisone 100 mg IV loading then 50 mg every 6 hours.
Cooling and paracetamol for fever; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (they raise free thyroid hormone). IV fluids with glucose (watch for hypoglycaemia and heart failure); consider thiamine.
Treat the precipitant aggressively, including empirical antibiotics after cultures when infection is possible.

sections.title: Rhythm, sedation and refractory storm
items: Target heart rate 130 per minute or less; stop or reduce beta-blockade if heart rate falls below 80, systolic BP below 80 mmHg or cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m2 or less (JTA/JES).
Beta-blocker contraindicated (asthma, decompensation on beta-blocker): diltiazem 60 to 90 mg orally every 6 hours (IV possible).
AF: rate control as above; anticoagulate by CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk; digoxin 0.125 to 0.25 mg IV with caution if renal function is adequate; cardiovert if haemodynamically unstable.
Sedation if needed: chlorpromazine 50 to 100 mg IM (also lowers temperature).
Adjuncts: cholestyramine 4 g orally three to four times daily; lithium 300 mg twice daily with level monitoring only on specialist advice when thionamides cannot be used.

No clinical improvement within 24 to 48 hours despite full therapy: reassess absorption and precipitant, then consider therapeutic plasma exchange, emergency thyroidectomy in a specialist centre, or ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Continuous ECG, BP, SpO2, temperature, fluid balance and capillary glucose. Improvement is usually seen within 24 to 72 hours.
FT4 and FT3 every 1 to 2 days (expect a progressive fall over days); TSH is not useful early.
CBC and liver tests on high-dose thionamides; any fever or sore throat needs an urgent neutrophil count (agranulocytosis).
Monitor potassium after high-dose glucocorticoids: thyrotoxic periodic paralysis can occur, especially in young Asian men.

sections.title: Step-down and definitive care
items: Once stable: stop iodine first, taper and stop steroids if adrenal insufficiency is not suspected, and reduce thionamide to about PTU 400 mg/day, methimazole 30 mg/day or carbimazole 40 mg/day. Continue beta-blockade while thyrotoxic.
Plan definitive treatment (radioiodine or thyroidectomy) before discharge. Radioiodine is usually deferred 2 to 3 months after iodine therapy.
Before discharge, teach adherence to antithyroid drugs and to stop them and get an urgent blood count for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Pregnancy: PTU in the first trimester, methimazole or carbimazole thereafter; involve obstetric and neonatal teams early.
Destructive thyroiditis (subacute, painless, amiodarone type 2) or thyroxine overdose: thionamides and iodine do not help; use beta-blockade, glucocorticoids and cholestyramine.
Suspected thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy or cardiogenic shock: echocardiography before or alongside beta-blockade; high-dose propranolol can precipitate collapse.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving iodine before the thionamide (can fuel further hormone synthesis).
Using aspirin for fever.
Waiting for thyroid function results before starting treatment.
Stopping thionamides early after the crisis settles, without a definitive treatment plan.

drugs.name: Propranolol
drugs.dose: 60 to 80 mg orally every 4 hours; IV 1 to 3 mg at no more than 1 mg/min, repeat once after 2 minutes
drugs.notes: Avoid or use cautiously in heart failure, hypotension or asthma.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.dose: 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 minute, then infusion titrated up to 200 mcg/kg/min
drugs.notes: Preferred when LV function or BP is a concern (short half-life).

drugs.name: Methimazole (thiamazole)
drugs.dose: 60 to 80 mg/day orally or via NG tube in divided doses
drugs.notes: Reduce to about 30 mg/day once stable.

drugs.name: Carbimazole
drugs.dose: 80 to 100 mg/day orally or via NG tube in divided doses
drugs.notes: Widely used in India; reduce to about 40 mg/day once stable.

drugs.name: Propylthiouracil
drugs.dose: 500 to 1000 mg loading dose, then 250 mg every 4 hours (oral, NG or rectal)
drugs.notes: Preferred in first-trimester pregnancy; avoid if liver tests exceed 3 times normal. Reduce to about 400 mg/day once stable.

drugs.name: Lugol's iodine or SSKI
drugs.dose: Lugol's 8 drops four times daily or SSKI 5 drops four times daily, diluted
drugs.notes: Start at least 1 hour after the thionamide. Stop once stable.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: 100 mg IV every 8 hours (JTA/JES) or 100 mg IV loading then 50 mg every 6 hours (ETA/BTA 2026)
drugs.notes: Dexamethasone 8 mg/day is an alternative. Taper once stable.

drugs.name: Cholestyramine
drugs.dose: 4 g orally three to four times daily

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours (maximum 4 g/day)
drugs.notes: Antipyretic of choice; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.
